item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q018_tal_effector_repeat_lengths","answer":"d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, and d4cj9a_ are classified together because SCOPe family a.298.1.1 is the TAL effector repeat family: all three domains are all-alpha TAL effector DNA-binding repeat arrays built from homologous helix-turn-helix repeat units. The large differences in sequence length mainly reflect how many near-identical TALE repeats were present in each crystallized or NMR construct, not a change to a different fold or to an unrelated evolutionary family. In SCOPe terms, they sit in class a, all-alpha proteins; fold a.298, TAL effector; superfamily a.298.1, TAL effector; and family a.298.1.1, TAL effector. The fold is the right structural comparison level for the repeated superhelical architecture, while the family level is still appropriate here because the repeats come from the same TALE lineage and share the same repeat-unit architecture even when one PDB entry contains only a minimal repeat fragment and another contains many repeats. The important caveat is that the SCOPe assignment says the repeat scaffold is homologous, not that the full chains are globally alignable end-to-end with a fixed length. Repeat copy number, N- and C-terminal truncation, and the repeat-variable diresidues can differ; the RVDs control base preference, so DNA specificity and any residue-level functional annotation should be transferred only repeat-by-repeat and in register. Likewise, a long TALE array is a useful structural template for the helical repeat scaffold of another TALE only after accounting for repeat number and phasing, not as a simple one-to-one template for the entire sequence.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
